text: SLURM applies defaults when a resource directive is omitted: --nodes defaults to 1, --ntasks defaults to one task per allocated node (not per job), and --cpus-per-task defaults to 1. Omitting a directive is not the same as requesting zero of that resource: it silently falls back to the default, which may be far below what the job actually needs. A job asking for 2 nodes and 4 tasks that only declares --nodes=2 will run with 2 tasks, not 4, because --ntasks was never set.

SLURM reads #SBATCH directive lines only from the top of the script, stopping at the first line that is not a comment or a directive. Any #SBATCH line placed after a real command (including a blank line followed by shell code) is silently ignored: sbatch still accepts the script, but the ignored directive never takes effect. All #SBATCH lines must appear before any executable command.

Unlike --nodes, --ntasks and --cpus-per-task, the directives --time, --mem and --gpus have no universal SLURM-wide default: omitting them means the resource is never requested, not that a sane default is assumed. A script that needs a walltime limit or a memory floor must declare --time and --mem explicitly.

A SLURM job array is declared with --array=START-END (for example --array=1-5 for five tasks indexed 1 through 5). Each array task sees its own index in the environment variable SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID. A script that also needs to run correctly outside an array context should default that variable when unset, for example idx=${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID:-1}.

Standard output and error paths are set with --output=PATH and --error=PATH. The pattern %j expands to the numeric job ID, so --output=logs/out_%j.txt gives each job run its own log file. If the target directory does not already exist, the script itself must create it (for example with mkdir -p logs) before SLURM can write to it.

GPUs are requested either with --gpus=N (a simple count) or with the more general --gres=gpu:N generic resource syntax; both are read by anvil's resource_fit check. The environment variable CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set by SLURM to the GPU indices allocated to the job; a script can print it to confirm which devices it was actually given.

A job that must wait for another job to finish successfully declares --dependency=afterok:JOBID, where JOBID is the numeric ID of the job it depends on. SLURM will not start the dependent job until the referenced job exits with status 0; if it exits with a non-zero status, afterok never releases the dependency.

A SLURM script that runs a workload inside an Apptainer container typically calls apptainer exec IMAGE.sif COMMAND, optionally binding a host directory into the container with --bind /host/path:/container/path. Scripts intended to run on nodes where Apptainer may not be installed should guard the call, for example with `command -v apptainer >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo NO_APPTAINER; exit 0; }`, so the job fails gracefully instead of erroring on a missing binary.
